segments.en: Letter 18 is written entirely in Yiddish — the only letter in this collection addressed to Avraham Dovid rather than Yitzchak Meir. It is a complete and practical guide to Breslov service: study the Rebbe's books like a Shulchan Aruch — extracting one clear practical law from every passage. Then pray and do hisbodidus every day, even for just a few minutes. Rabbi Shimshon's credential here is powerful: he says his counsel comes not from faith without knowledge, but from personal, lived clarification through his own trials and battles over many years.

Letter 19 contains a remarkable Breslov teaching from Chayay Moharan: the Rebbe himself said he would have wanted his followers to have a steady livelihood without confusion — so they could engage in other spiritual services. The corollary: those who support Rabbi Shimshon financially during his travels are freeing him to serve. The Uman fellowship's distress at his potential departure is deeply moving — R' Mordechai Polsky "literally cannot live in peace for even one day" without their study sessions together.

Letter 20 presses Yitzchak Meir on the outreach work and contains a beautiful teaching: even though much of what he received from the Rebbe's light has been forgotten — the rishimah tovah (good impression) that remains is more precious than all worldly success, for in the end only that will remain.

Letter 21 consoles a person in severe financial trial with the teaching that in the end of days, drawing close to holiness does not come cheaply. The Patriarchs' trials were sweetened — how much more will ours be, in the merit of the Tzadik who suffered for us. One must wait with patience and hope.

Letter 22 is the most comprehensive and doctrinally rich letter of this installment — essentially a complete theology of the Breslov path. It covers: the Omer-period as a universal template for spiritual descent after initial arousal; the Vav-within-the-Aleph teaching (humiliation and bloodshed as the channel of connection to the Tzadik); the folly of opining on communal matters before undergoing sufficient self-nullification; and the call to cast away one's own intellect and enter the "school" of the Rebbe's books.

Letter 23 opens the new section of Letters to His Son — a completely different register. Rabbi Shimshon is now writing as a father to his child. The surviving fragment covers livelihood and healing from one single divine source, charity as a remedy, joy as healing, and the teaching of "In distress You have broadened me." Both the beginning and the continuation of this letter are missing from the manuscript.
